specPoints.text: understand why a current in a resistor results in the electrical transfer of energy and an increase in temperature, and how this can be used in a variety of domestic contexts

primer.text: Push a current through a resistor and the resistor warms up — the electrical transfer of energy shows itself as heat. Free electrons jostling through the wire collide and hand over energy, some of which escapes to the surroundings. Far from being a nuisance, that heating effect runs heaters, ovens, hobs, toasters and kettles.

lessons.title: The heating effect of a current
lessons.opening: Current is a stream of charge, and driving it through a resistor takes work. That work appears as heat: the drifting electrons collide inside the wire, the temperature climbs, and some energy dissipates into the room. Domestic appliances exploit the effect deliberately, turning a glowing element into a hob, a toaster or a kettle.
keyPoints: A current through a resistor or wire transfers energy electrically and warms it.
Free electrons colliding inside the wire raise its temperature.
Some of that energy dissipates into the surroundings by heating.
Domestic appliances put the heating effect to work: heaters, ovens, hobs, toasters and kettles.

low.restatement: Current passing through a resistor makes it hot, because the moving electrons collide inside the wire.
low.analogy: A crowded corridor: people (electrons) bumping into each other and the walls warms everyone up.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism — collisions of free electrons — whenever a question asks why a resistor heats.

medium.restatement: The same transfer that heats a useful element also dissipates into the surroundings, so every design trades heat delivered against heat lost.
medium.analogy: A kettle versus a phone charger: one sells the heat, the other apologises for it.
medium.examPointer: Domestic-context questions expect named appliances, not just 'gets hot'.

check.stem: The temperature of a current-carrying resistor rises because:

options.explanation: Protons stay fixed in the lattice; only electrons drift.

options.text: moving electrons collide inside the wire
options.explanation: The drifting free electrons transfer energy in collisions, raising the temperature.
Charge is never generated; it only flows.
The electrical transfer warms, not cools.

check.stem: Energy delivered to a resistor ends up:

options.explanation: The resistor does not store charge.
Only some components glow; the general outcome is heat.
Energy is conserved, never destroyed.

options.text: partly dissipated to the surroundings as heat
options.explanation: Some of the transferred energy escapes to the surroundings by heating.

check.stem: Which appliance is deliberately built around the heating effect?

options.explanation: Toasters, kettles, heaters, ovens and hobs all exploit the heating effect.
An LED is built to avoid heating.
A clock is an electronic, not a heating, device.
A radio is an electronic device.
Current is a flow, not a store.
Current is a flow of charge, not a force.

options.text: the rate of flow of charge
options.explanation: That is the definition the note relies on.
Energy is measured in joules, current in amperes.

check.stem: A hob heating element warms a pan mainly by:

options.explanation: The pan does not rub the element.

options.text: electrical transfer of energy in the element
options.explanation: The current in the resistive element transfers energy that then heats the pan.
No light is involved.
Static is unrelated to the mains element.

check.stem: Name three domestic appliances that use the heating effect.
check.modelAnswer: Electric heaters, ovens, hobs, toasters and kettles — any three of these.

check.stem: Why does a resistor's temperature rise when current flows?
check.modelAnswer: The free electrons drift through the lattice and collide, transferring energy to the wire, which warms up and dissipates some heat to the surroundings.

check.stem: Explain why the heating effect counts as useful in a kettle but wasteful in long cables.
check.modelAnswer: In a kettle the warmed element is the entire point of the device, while in a cable the heat only dissipates into the room, wasting energy and risking the insulation.

check.stem: An electric hob warms a pan. Trace the energy pathway from the mains to the pan.
check.modelAnswer: Mains current flows through the resistive element; the electrical transfer raises the element's temperature; the hot element then heats the pan by contact.

glossary.definition: The rise in temperature produced when a current transfers energy in a resistor.
To spread energy out to the surroundings, often as unwanted heat.
The mobile electrons in a metal that drift and carry the current.
